tldr: In mega-scale reinforcement learning with over one million parallel simulation environments, the authors propose SGS, a sampling method that focuses training on tasks with intermediate success rates where the policy can actually improve. Without manual reward shaping or human demonstrations, it achieves extremely challenging quadruped locomotion and high-precision assembly.
hero_caption: An overview of this work. By focusing training on task configurations along the frontier of the policy's capabilities, it successfully learns diverse skills using only simple, shared rewards—from quadruped locomotion traversing complex terrains to contact-rich assembly like bolt-and-nut threading. The learned policies are further distilled into RGB image-based models and achieve zero-shot transfer to real robots.
overview:
Combining simulation and reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising route to teach robots agile locomotion and dexterous manipulation. Traditionally, however, current RL pipelines rely heavily on per-task engineered reward shaping, human demonstrations, or hand-crafted curricula. Recently, pairing massively parallel simulation with diverse simulator resets has helped reduce this engineering burden.

Yet scaling this paradigm to more precise or dynamic tasks runs into a serious bottleneck. Uniform sampling over reset states wastes a huge fraction of training runs on configurations the policy has already mastered or cannot yet attempt. As a result, increasing the number of parallel environments from tens of thousands up to a million dilutes the learning signal in each batch, blunting the benefits of scaling.

To fix this, the authors introduce Success Guided Sampling (SGS), a simple adaptive sampler. SGS tracks recent success rates for each configuration and concentrates resources on tasks at the frontier of capability—where success rates are neither too low nor too high. This allows mega-scale RL to make the most of its batch experience, even at an unprecedented scale of up to $2^{20}$ (over one million) parallel environments.

Experiments evaluate full-body quadruped locomotion across 13 challenging terrains and high-precision assembly involving threading a nut onto a bolt. While prior methods fail or plateau, SGS scales monotonically with the number of environments and achieves decisive success rates. Furthermore, distilling the policies into RGB image-based models enables successful zero-shot transfer to real dual-arm and single-arm robots.
contributions: Proposed Success Guided Sampling (SGS), a simple adaptive sampler driven by success rates, and demonstrated its effectiveness in mega-scale reinforcement learning with up to ~1 million parallel environments.

Acquired a single quadruped locomotion policy covering 13 challenging terrains and 6 high-precision assembly policies using only simple, domain-wide reward functions, without per-task reward shaping or demonstrations.

Observed steady scaling laws where performance increases as the number of parallel environments grows in both quadruped locomotion and nut threading, significantly outperforming baselines like uniform sampling and PLR.
Distilled the learned manipulation policies into RGB image-based policies via DAgger and achieved successful zero-shot transfer to real hardware.

sections.heading: Why large-scale simulation alone is not enough
sections.summary: RL with massively parallel simulation is promising, but traditional pipelines rely on per-task reward engineering and demonstrations. While diverse reset distributions relieve manual tuning, uniform sampling wastes experience on configurations that are already mastered or impossible. This section introduces SGS to focus exploration on tasks at the right difficulty level based on success rates.
sections.details:
When applying reinforcement learning to robots, the biggest bottleneck has been heavy, per-task engineering. Fine-tuning reward functions, building manual curricula, and collecting demonstrations create massive human overhead for every new task.

To overcome this, recent work uses diverse simulator reset distributions that initialize agents from intermediate states across the task. This significantly mitigates the exploration challenge, but it introduces a new question: how should environments be allocated across these reset states?

Under standard uniform sampling, environments are assigned equally across all initial states. This means the policy spends equal effort on states it has already mastered and states that are far beyond its current capabilities. Consequently, increasing the number of parallel environments dilutes the informative gradient signals in the batch, negating the expected benefits of parallelism.

Success Guided Sampling (SGS) solves this by tracking the current success rate of each configuration and automatically shifting environment allocation toward settings that are neither too easy nor too hard. Without any manual curriculum engineering, it continuously supplies the policy with the most productive tasks as it learns.

sections.heading: Roots in reset distributions and curriculum learning
sections.summary: This work sits at the intersection of four areas: sim-to-real RL, reset distributions for exploration, scaling parallel simulation, and automated curriculum learning. Rather than inventing complex new principles, SGS couples a clean, success-guided sampling idea with mega-scale RL.
sections.details:
To understand the position of this work, consider four related research areas:

- Sim-to-real reinforcement learning: Using algorithms like PPO to train policies in massively parallel simulation before deploying them on physical robots. However, many successful applications still depend on task-specific rewards or demonstrations.
- Reset distributions for exploration: Methods that reverse-curriculum from near-goal states or demonstrations, as well as procedural approaches like OmniReset that generate diverse geometric initial states. SGS builds on top of such reset candidate pools.
- Scaling parallel RL: GPU-accelerated parallel simulators allow training across tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of environments. Yet as batch sizes grow massive, data redundancy and inefficient exploration become major challenges.
- Automated curriculum learning and task sampling: Methods that select tasks based on learner progress, such as PLR using TD errors or SFL (Sampling for Learnability) based on $p(1-p)$ success rates.

SGS shares the intuition of prioritizing intermediate success rates seen in methods like SFL. However, SGS uses a smooth Beta-kernel parameterization to flexibly shift the target success rate while ensuring every configuration retains a non-zero sampling probability. Crucially, the unique contribution of this paper is demonstrating that this simple sampler unlocks dramatic scaling benefits at the unprecedented scale of roughly one million parallel environments.

sections.heading: How SGS works and how mega-scale RL is designed
sections.summary: SGS dynamically adjusts sampling probabilities across a predefined set of task configurations using recent success rates. A Beta kernel assigns high weight to tasks with intermediate success rates while retaining non-zero probabilities for all tasks. In addition, domain-wide uniform, simple reward functions are used without per-task tuning.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Task Configurations
The robot control problem is formulated as a goal-conditioned Markov Decision Process (MDP). A task configuration is defined as $	au=(s_{0}, g, e)$, comprising an initial state $s_{0}$, a goal $g$, and environment parameters $e$ (such as terrain geometry or asset layouts).
- Quadruped Locomotion: Specifies terrain type and geometry, initial robot pose, and target navigation pose.
- Manipulation: Specifies assembly task, initial state, and receptacle pose. Initial states fall into three stages: Near-Goal, Stable Grasp, and workspace Reaching.

### 3.2 Success Guided Sampling (SGS)
The core intuition of SGS is to concentrate practice on tasks that are just within reach. It begins with a fixed pool of $N$ task configurations (32,768 for manipulation and 104,000 for locomotion).
During training, a ring buffer stores the binary success/failure outcomes of the most recent $H=100$ episodes for each configuration, yielding an empirical success rate $p_{i}$.
Next, each configuration's score $w_{i}$ is computed using a Beta kernel defined by a target mode $t$ and concentration $\kappa$, which forms logits $\ell_{i}$:
A small epsilon $\epsilon > 0$ is added so that configurations with success rates of 0 or 1 never drop to zero probability. This ensures the robot periodically revisits unattempted or mastered tasks to refresh their success estimates. Finally, a softmax function with temperature $T$ converts these logits into sampling probabilities.

### 3.3 Algorithmic Design for Mega-Scale RL
Two key design choices make SGS effective:
- Simple, Domain-Wide Rewards: A single shared reward function is used across all locomotion terrains, and another single function across all manipulation tasks. The sparse terminal success reward (+1) dominates, with minimal step-wise regularization terms and no manual reward shaping.
- Scaling Parallel Environments: By allocating environments to configurations that produce useful learning gradients, the method avoids wasted compute as parallel environment counts scale up, maintaining high learning signal density.

sections.heading: Dominant scaling across one million environments and real-world deployment
sections.summary: Evaluations in quadruped locomotion and nut threading at up to ~1 million parallel environments demonstrate that SGS outperforms baselines and scales monotonically. It also learns efficiently in smaller settings, and distillation into RGB-based policies enables successful zero-shot transfer to real robots.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 Experimental Setup
For locomotion, an ANYmal-D quadruped is trained to traverse 13 difficult terrains—including floating pillars and stepping stones—from scratch with a single policy. Unlike prior pipelines that distill separate expert policies, this approach trains one universal policy directly.
For manipulation, the NIST assembly board is evaluated (6 tasks on a UR5e, and bolt-and-nut threading on a Franka Panda). The bolt-and-nut task is contact-rich, requiring the robot to thread an M16 nut down roughly 6.5 full revolutions.

### 4.3 Scaling Performance (Q1)
Scaling behavior with increasing parallel environments was compared against uniform sampling, a manual curriculum, and PLR (Prioritized Level Replay).
At $2^{20}$ (over one million) parallel environments, SGS reached an average success rate of 73% in locomotion, whereas PLR reached only 54%. Even more striking was Franka nut threading: uniform sampling achieved 6% and PLR achieved 5% (both failing almost completely), while SGS achieved a 70% success rate. Only SGS demonstrated monotonic scaling as environment counts increased.

### 4.4 Capability Acquisition in Smaller Environments (Q2)
SGS excels not only at mega-scale, but also in smaller regimes like 4,096 environments. In locomotion, where uniform baselines failed to make any progress, SGS extracted informative training signals from limited steps through adaptive sampling, achieving meaningful success rates.

### 4.5 Zero-Shot Real-World Transfer (Q3)
A teacher policy trained on simulated point clouds was distilled into an RGB-based student policy using DAgger. Deploying this student policy directly onto a real UR5e robot resulted in successful execution of nut threading, peg insertion, and gear meshing. The policy spontaneously demonstrated robust behaviors, such as retrying after misses and flicking the nut with its fingers to adjust its orientation through non-prehensile manipulation.

captions.F7: Evolution of SGS sampling distributions over training. Early on, the policy explores all configurations uniformly; in the middle stage, it focuses on jumping between floating pillars of equal height; toward the end, sampling mass shifts automatically to the hardest transitions across pillars with large height differences.
captions.F6: Nut threading task using the Franka robot. The task demands high precision: aligning the nut with tight clearances and threading it down approximately 6.5 rotations. In 1 million parallel environments, where prior methods collapse to 5–6%, SGS reaches a 70% success rate.
captions.F4: Zero-shot deployment of the RGB image-based policy on a real UR5e. Top: nut threading; middle: peg insertion; bottom: gear insertion. Precision assembly succeeds without any real-world fine-tuning or extra data collection.

sections.heading: Limitations of SGS and future directions
sections.summary: SGS has three main limitations: it requires maintaining a discrete set of task configurations, it does not dynamically generate reset candidates on its own, and a sim-to-real performance gap still remains.
sections.details:
The paper outlines three main limitations:

- Managing discrete task cells: SGS stores success statistics across a fixed set of $N$ discrete configurations. While tens of thousands to a hundred thousand cells fit easily in memory, continuous or broader task spaces will require learned value estimators or hierarchical representations.
- No procedural reset generation: SGS only samples intelligently from an existing pool; it does not generate candidates itself. Because it relies on external reset generators like OmniReset, integrating SGS with mechanisms that actively determine which configurations to propose is an open challenge.
- Sim-to-real gap: Despite achieving strong simulation performance, real-world success rates still lag behind simulator metrics. Closing this gap completely remains an area for future work.

sections.heading: Takeaway: A balanced data diet unlocks RL scaling
sections.summary: By concentrating on tasks with intermediate success rates, SGS enables policies to learn complex locomotion and high-precision assembly without manual reward shaping or hand-crafted curricula. True scaling comes not just from adding more environments, but from adaptively deciding what the robot practices.
sections.details:
This study clearly shows that what a policy is fed during mega-scale RL—its data diet and allocation—is critically important.

Without depending on complex reward shaping or human demonstrations, combining diverse resets with simple success-guided sampling solves both multi-terrain quadruped locomotion and millimeter-precision assembly within a unified pipeline. Furthermore, distilling to RGB policies demonstrates end-to-end real-world viability.

These findings strongly suggest that adaptive data sampling is an essential component for training general-purpose robot controllers, unlocking capabilities that raw compute scaling alone could not achieve.

sections.heading: Appendix: Discovering gripper friction as the sim-to-real culprit
sections.summary: The appendix provides detailed ablation studies. In particular, it reveals that an unrealistically high gripper friction coefficient ($\mu=100$) used in prior work induced physically impossible grasps, creating a major obstacle for sim-to-real transfer.
sections.details:
### Gripper Friction and the Reality Gap
The authors share a valuable insight regarding sim-to-real transfer. Prior work like OmniReset set the Robotiq gripper pad friction to an extreme value of $\mu=100$ to stabilize grasping during training.
However, this caused objects to stick as soon as they touched the edge of a pad, producing unrealistic grasps impossible in the real world. This flaw created a severe transfer gap on physical hardware.
Testing lower friction values revealed that while too low a value prevents learning from scratch, $\mu=2$ is the lower bound that maintains stable learning. Adopting $\mu=2$ promoted physically grounded grasps and enabled smooth real-world transfer.

### Gravity Curricula Are Unnecessary
While initial manipulation experiments used a curriculum that gradually increased gravity from zero, ablations showed that SGS at 1 million environments achieves virtually identical success rates (~70%) without any gravity curriculum, reinforcing the simplicity of the method.

captions.F8: Examples of unrealistic grasps caused by setting gripper friction to $\mu=100$. Objects stick unnaturally even when barely hooked on the tip of the pad, which directly caused failures when transferring the policy to real hardware.

takeaways: In mega-scale parallel RL, simply adding environments is not enough; compute must be concentrated on tasks of intermediate difficulty suited to the policy's current capabilities.
Without manual reward shaping or human demonstrations, diverse reset distributions paired with Success Guided Sampling (SGS) can learn contact-rich assembly and complex locomotion from scratch.
Setting simulator parameters like gripper friction to unrealistic values (e.g., $\mu=100$) to stabilize learning can severely compromise sim-to-real transfer.
Distilling point-cloud teacher policies into RGB student models using DAgger achieves zero-shot real-robot transfer for precision assembly without additional real-world data.
limitations: Tracking task configurations as a predefined discrete set makes it difficult to scale directly to continuous or vastly larger task parameter spaces.
SGS does not generate reset configurations on its own; it relies on an external pool produced by methods such as OmniReset.
Although zero-shot transfer succeeded on real hardware, real-world success rates remain lower than simulation performance, leaving a sim-to-real gap to be addressed.
